title: Calculus
summary: Single-variable calculus from functions and limits through derivatives, integrals, sequences and series, then a first step into functions of two variables, complex numbers and double integrals. The quarter has 24 two-hour lectures, three a week, with one central topic per week, pre-lecture videos and polling quizzes in class. Practice is ungraded homework from the Stewart textbook and Grasple; the grade comes from a midterm and an endterm, both written by hand without a calculator.

basis.description: Slide text of Lectures 1 to 23 of the course as taught under the old code CSE1200, the official CSE1200 course description, and the past papers from 2019 to 2025. Time shares count content slides; Lecture 24 (exam training) is left out.
basis.caveat: The curriculum note says CSE1200 was renamed CSE12A for 2026-27 with the content unchanged, still in year 1, quarter 2. Lecture 13 is split by its slides: the first half finishes the convergence tests, the second half starts power series.

topics.name: Functions, limits and asymptotes
know: Domain, range and inverse of a one-to-one function, and how restricting the domain decides which branch of the inverse you take
arcsin, arccos and arctan with their ranges, and how to turn expressions such as cos(2 arcsin(x)) into algebra with a right-angled triangle or a double-angle identity
Continuity, the intermediate value theorem, and the epsilon-delta definition of a limit, including one-sided limits
Techniques for 0/0: cancelling common factors, the square-root (conjugate) trick, the squeeze theorem and the standard limits such as sin(x)/x as x goes to 0
Horizontal, vertical and oblique asymptotes, and why a factor that cancels gives a hole instead of a vertical asymptote
L'Hospital's rule, the conditions under which it may be used, and rewriting 0 times infinity, 1^infinity, 0^0 and infinity minus infinity into a quotient first
The exam conventions: a limit is a finite value, plus or minus infinity, or DNE
do: Compute limits at a point and at plus and minus infinity without a calculator
Find every asymptote of a rational or root function, checking plus and minus infinity separately
Give the formula and the domain of the inverse of a quadratic on a restricted interval
Evaluate power limits such as (1 + ln(x))^(1/(x^2 - 1)) by taking the logarithm and applying l'Hospital
pitfalls: Using l'Hospital where the limit of the quotient of derivatives does not exist: the Midterm 2025 model answer needs a squeeze argument instead
Missing an oblique asymptote at minus infinity: when x is negative, taking x^3 inside a square root flips the sign
Writing infinity when the left and right limits differ, where the answer is DNE

topics.name: Derivatives and their applications
lectures: Lecture 5 - Implicit Differentiation and Newton's Method
know: The derivative as a limit of difference quotients, differentiability, and the product, quotient and chain rules
Tangent line and linearisation L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a), and differentials for estimating an error
Critical points, the extreme value theorem and the closed interval method for absolute extremes
The mean value theorem and its corollary that f' = 0 on an interval means f is constant
Implicit differentiation, logarithmic differentiation (as for x^x) and the derivatives of the inverse trigonometric functions
Newton's method: the iteration formula, its picture with tangent lines, and when it converges
do: Approximate a value such as the cube root of 217 with a well-chosen linearisation
Find the absolute maximum and minimum of a function on a closed interval
Find horizontal or vertical tangents of an implicitly defined curve
Sketch two Newton steps on a given graph
pitfalls: Forgetting the end points of the interval when listing candidates for an absolute extreme
Including the origin when asked for the top of a curve: the solution has to exclude points where the derivative equation is trivially satisfied

topics.name: Integration techniques and improper integrals
lectures: Lecture 7 - Integrals and the Substitution Rule
know: Riemann sums, the properties of the definite integral and both parts of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
Standard antiderivatives and the substitution rule, including changing the bounds of a definite integral
Integration by parts, the LIATE heuristic, integrals that return to themselves (e^x cos(x)) and reduction formulas
Even and odd functions: an odd integrand over a symmetric interval integrates to 0
Improper integrals of type 1 (infinite bound) and type 2 (unbounded integrand), the standard cases 1/x^p, and the comparison test
The exam convention: an integral is either its value or DIV
do: Evaluate an integral that needs a substitution followed by integration by parts
Compute the area between two curves after finding their intersection points
Decide whether an improper integral converges, splitting it at every problem point
Use the Fundamental Theorem to differentiate a function defined as an integral
pitfalls: Not splitting an integral at an asymptote inside the interval: the Midterm 2025 integral has both an infinite bound and an asymptote at u = 0
Treating an integral over the whole real line as one limit; both separate limits must exist

topics.name: Sequences and convergence of series
lectures: Lecture 12 - Alternating Series and Comparison Test
Lecture 13 - Ratio Test and Power Series
know: Limits of explicit and recursive sequences, fixed points, simple iteration and the monotone convergence theorem
Series as limits of partial sums; geometric series and when they converge; p-series
The divergence test, integral test, comparison and limit comparison tests, alternating series test and ratio test, with the conditions of each
Absolute convergence, conditional convergence and divergence (AC, CC or D)
Error bounds on partial sums from the integral test, the alternating series test and comparison
do: Prove a recursive sequence is monotone and bounded by induction, then find its limit as the correct fixed point
Classify a series as AC, CC or D and name the test and the conditions you checked
Sum a geometric series, or a sum of two geometric series
Approximate the sum of a series to a given error and justify the bound
pitfalls: Choosing the wrong root of L = g(L) for a recursive sequence; check which fixed point the sequence can actually reach
Applying the alternating series test without checking that the terms decrease, or calling a series CC without showing that the absolute series diverges

topics.name: Power series and Taylor series
lectures: Lecture 13 - Ratio Test and Power Series
know: Centre, radius and interval of convergence of a power series, found with the ratio test, and the separate check of both end points
Building series from 1/(1 - x) by substitution, multiplication, differentiation and integration term by term
The Maclaurin series of e^x, sin(x), cos(x), ln(1 + x), arctan(x) and the binomial series, which you need to know by heart
Taylor coefficients: the coefficient of x^n is f^(n)(0)/n!
Taylor polynomials, Taylor's inequality and the Lagrange remainder
do: Find the interval of convergence of a given power series, end points included or excluded with a reason
Write the Taylor series at 0 of an antiderivative of e^(x^2) or a similar function
Approximate a definite integral to a given error using a series and justify the bound
Read off a high derivative such as f^(9)(0) from a series
Sum a series such as the sum of n/2^(n-1) by differentiating a geometric series
pitfalls: Forgetting to test the end points: the papers remind you every time, and the Endterm 2025 grading guide gives a point for each end point
Forgetting the n! when going from a series coefficient to a derivative value

topics.name: Functions of several variables and gradients
know: Vectors: length, dot product and the cosine of the angle between two vectors
Maximal domain, graph, level curves and contour plots of a function of two variables
Limits in two variables and how to show that one does not exist along different paths
Partial derivatives, higher partials and Clairaut's theorem
Tangent plane, linearisation in two variables and differentiability
The multivariable chain rule, the gradient, the directional derivative D_u f = grad f . u with u a unit vector, and the gradient as the direction of steepest ascent
do: Compute a gradient and a directional derivative at a point
Match functions to contour plots by reasoning about their level sets
Find the slope of a level curve at a point with the gradient or implicit differentiation
Find the unit vector along which the function decreases fastest
pitfalls: Using the direction vector without normalising it first
Mixing up the gradient (a vector) with the directional derivative (a number)

topics.name: Extrema of functions of two variables
know: Critical points as solutions of grad f = 0
The second derivatives test with D = f_xx f_yy - (f_xy)^2: local minimum, local maximum, saddle point or inconclusive
The extreme value theorem for closed and bounded regions
The closed and bounded region method: interior critical points, each boundary piece as a one-variable problem, and the corner points
do: Find and classify the interior critical points on a triangle or half-disc
Find the absolute maximum and minimum on that region by checking every edge and corner
Read a local minimum off a plot of normalised gradient vectors
pitfalls: Leaving out the corner points of the region; the Endterm 2025 grading guide gives a separate point for them
Counting a saddle point as a candidate for an absolute extreme

topics.name: Complex numbers
know: Arithmetic with complex numbers, the conjugate, and division by multiplying with the conjugate
Modulus, argument, polar form r(cos(theta) + i sin(theta)) and the exponential form r e^(i theta)
Euler's formula and De Moivre's rule, and how they give double and triple angle formulas
The n-th roots of a complex number: n roots on a circle, spaced 2 pi/n apart
The fundamental theorem of algebra and the fact that the non-real roots of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs
do: Solve equations such as (z - 2)^3 = -8 and give the roots as a + bi or draw them in the plane
Compute powers and quotients with the polar form
Derive a trigonometric identity from Euler's formula, or prove Euler's formula with power series
pitfalls: Stopping after one root: the grading guide gives a point for the correct number of solutions
Taking the argument from arctan(b/a) without checking the quadrant

topics.name: Double integrals
know: The double integral as a limit of Riemann sums in two variables, and its meaning as volume
Fubini's theorem: iterated integrals over a rectangle in either order, and separable integrands
Type I and type II regions, and how to describe a region with variable bounds
Reversing the order of integration, and splitting a region that is neither type into simple pieces
do: Sketch a region bounded by curves and find the intersection points
Set up and evaluate a double integral over a triangle, trapezoid or curved region
Split an irregular region into simple parts, or subtract simpler regions from a larger one
pitfalls: Choosing an order of integration that forces a split when the other order needs none
Bounds that do not match the region; in the Endterm 2025 grading guide the bounds carry 2 of the 5 points

prerequisites: Fluent secondary-school algebra: factoring polynomials, long division, rules for exponents, roots and logarithms
Trigonometry: exact values on the unit circle and the double-angle identities
The standard derivative rules, which Lecture 4 only recaps
Proof by induction and the idea of a function as a relation, from Reasoning & Logic
Basic vectors in two and three dimensions, recapped in Lecture 16
practical: No labs or graded assignments. Each lecture has a pre-lecture video and exercises that the lecture assumes you have done, plus ungraded homework from the Stewart textbook and on Grasple, which gives instant feedback on basic skills.
studyAdvice: Power series and Taylor series take 9 percent of the lectures but about a quarter of all exam points, mostly in open questions on the endterm and resit. Give them far more practice time than their slides suggest.
For the midterm (Lectures 1 to 10), drill limits, asymptotes, inverse functions and integrals: these carry most of the points on Midterm 2024 and Midterm 2025.
Learn the standard Maclaurin series and the convergence tests by heart. The 2025 papers mention no formula sheet, and Midterm 2025 explicitly banned one.
Practise without a calculator and under time pressure: about 14 short questions in two hours, where only the final answer counts.

Write out the full procedures for the recurring open questions (interval of convergence, extremes on a region, double integral, series approximation with an error bound) until you can follow each step without notes.
Do not skip the last two weeks: complex numbers, extrema in two variables and double integrals each come back as an open question on every endterm and resit.
